faqs.question: How many sentences should I say before I actually ask her to marry me?
faqs.answer: Four is our working rule, and it is editorial judgement rather than a measured result. What is measured is the rate: conversational English runs at about 196 words per minute, so 45 to 90 words of preamble is only 14 to 28 seconds of speech.

faqs.question: Is a two-minute proposal speech too long?
faqs.answer: At the 196 words-per-minute conversational rate, two minutes is roughly 390 words — far past the point where the listener has worked out what is coming. If you want two minutes of talking, say the four sentences, ask, and spend the rest of it afterwards.

faqs.question: How many words should a proposal message on WhatsApp be?
faqs.answer: About 60, which is three sentences at the roughly 20-word modern English sentence average. That ceiling is our judgement, not a measurement — font size and handset change where a message truncates, and we have not measured it on any particular phone.

faqs.question: Does a longer proposal make it sound more sincere?
faqs.answer: Length does buy believability, but for factual claims rather than feelings. In one EEG study of 105 people, long notes were accepted as true 53.6% of the time against 41.0% for short ones — and a proposal is not a claim anyone is auditing.

faqs.question: How long should a proposal letter be?
faqs.answer: Measure it in time, not words: one sitting of 15 to 20 minutes, which is the session length used in the expressive writing paradigm. A letter is the one form where length is permitted, because there the length is doing work for the writer.

faqs.question: Should a proposal letter be handwritten or typed?
faqs.answer: Either works for length purposes, because the limit is the sitting rather than the page. Handwriting simply produces fewer words in the same 15 to 20 minutes, which usually makes a tighter letter.

faqs.question: How many photos can I put on a proposal page before it gets too long?
faqs.answer: Keep the page to three to five screens and let the photos fit inside that — our judgement, not a measured number. The first thing to cut is duplicates: three shots of one evening is one photo.

faqs.question: What should I cut first if my proposal is too long?
faqs.answer: The history. How you met is almost always the longest block in a draft and it is a story for after the yes. After that, cut stacked adjectives — two is a choice, four is nerves.

faqs.question: Is it bad to propose in just one sentence?
faqs.answer: No. If you are in the same room and you already know the answer, one spoken sentence beats every longer format, including ours. Length is for distance, for a story worth scrolling, or for something you want reopened later.

faqs.question: How long does it take people to finish building a page like this?
faqs.answer: Sampled on the apology dashboard template, the median gap between a page's first save and its last edit is 2.2 hours, n=1,375. That is a platform figure about building, not about proposals specifically — we have no proposal-specific measurement.

faqs.question: Does length matter more if she reads it on her phone?
faqs.answer: It matters, and most of this traffic is on a phone: 48.3% of views across 21 page types are on one, 27,499 of 56,886. For the reading conditions themselves — first screen, interruptions — see our post on building an online proposal for a girlfriend.

faqs.question: When is Propose Day 2027, and does the date change the right length?
faqs.answer: Propose Day 2027 falls on Monday 8 February, the second day of Valentine week, with Rose Day on Sunday 7 February. The date does not change any of the four limits, though a working Monday argues for the shorter message rather than the longer page.

article.contentMarkdown:
# How Long Should a Marriage Proposal Be? Four Forms, Four Answers

Short enough that the question arrives before the listener starts waiting for it — and the number depends on which of four forms you are in. Spoken: under a minute, question inside the first four sentences. A written message: about 60 words, before a scroll.

A letter: one unhurried sitting of 15 to 20 minutes. A built page: three to five screens.

Two of our own numbers shape all four. Platform-wide across 21 page types, 48.3% of shared pages are opened on a phone (27,499 of 56,886 views), so most of these words land on a small screen. The median gap between a page's first save and its last edit is 2.2 hours — sampled on the apology dashboard template, n=1,375 — which says people draft, leave, and come back.

Below: each form's limit, where each number comes from, and where one sentence beats all of it.

## What "how long" means when you are measuring a proposal

Proposal length is not one measurement but four: seconds before the question in a spoken ask, words before a scroll in a message, minutes of writing in a letter, and screens in a built page.

Those units do not convert into each other, which is why a single word count is useless advice. Sixty words is a complete message and a thin letter.

What all four share is the position of the question rather than the size of the wrapper. Everything before "will you marry me" is preamble, and preamble is the part you can measure and cut.

## Why the question has to land before the story does

Conversational English runs at roughly 196 words per minute. Yuan, Liberman and Cieri measured that across 2,438 word-aligned Switchboard telephone conversations, with individual conversations ranging from 111 to 291 WPM, in [their Interspeech 2006 study of speaking rate in conversation](https://www.isca-archive.org/interspeech_2006/yuan06_interspeech.html). Strip out the silences and the "net" rate rises to 236 WPM.

Two things follow. A 45-to-90-word preamble is 14 to 28 seconds of real speech — much shorter than it feels while you are holding a ring.

The same study found speaking rate climbs sharply across turns of one to seven words before levelling off, meaning short utterances are delivered more slowly per word. Your final four-word sentence takes longer than the arithmetic predicts. It is the one sentence that should.

The rule about putting the question inside the first four sentences is editorial judgement, not a measured result. What is measured is the rate. The sentence count is our call about where a listener stops listening and starts waiting.

## Four forms, four length limits

Each form gets the same four fields in the same order: what length means there, the limit, where the number came from, and what to cut first.

### 1. The spoken ask — under a minute, question by sentence four

**What length means here:** seconds of speech before the question, not total words.

**The limit:** 45 to 90 words of preamble, then ask. Under 60 seconds from first word to question mark.

**Where the number comes from:** the 196 WPM conversational rate above puts 45 to 90 words at 14 to 28 seconds; doubling that for nerves and pauses still lands under a minute. The four-sentence rule is editorial judgement.

**Cut first:** the history. Where you met is a story for afterwards, and it is almost always the longest block in the draft.

### 2. The written message — about 60 words, three sentences

**What length means here:** words visible before the reader's thumb has to move.

**The limit:** around 60 words, which is three sentences of about 20.

**Where the number comes from:** 20 words is the modern English sentence average recorded in DuBay's survey of readability research, which traces Sherman's counts from 50 words per sentence in pre-Elizabethan prose to 29 in Victorian and about 20 today. The 60-word ceiling is editorial judgement — screen size and font settings move it, and we have not measured where a message truncates on any handset.

**Cut first:** adjectives stacked on one noun. Two is a choice; four is nerves.

### 3. The letter — one sitting of 15 to 20 minutes

**What length means here:** time spent writing, not words produced — the one form measured from the writer's end.

**The limit:** a single session of 15 to 20 minutes. Stop when the session stops, not when the page fills up.

**Where the number comes from:** the expressive writing paradigm, in which participants write about emotional events for 15 to 20 minutes across three to five occasions, summarised in [Baikie and Wilhelm's 2005 review in Advances in Psychiatric Treatment](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/advances-in-psychiatric-treatment/article/emotional-and-physical-health-benefits-of-expressive-writing/ED2976A61F5DE56B46F07A1CE9EA9F9F). Note exactly what that measures: benefit to the person writing.

**Cut first:** nothing. A letter is where length is permitted, because there the length works for you rather than on the reader. It is also why a letter should not be the whole proposal — hand it over after the question, not instead of it.

### 4. The built page — three to five screens

**What length means here:** screens, not words. Nobody counts words on a page they are scrolling.

**The limit:** three to five screens, with the question on the first one.

**Where the number comes from:** editorial judgement. We could not obtain an open reading-rate figure to derive it from — the two standard sources were behind bot walls — so this is an opinion anchored on two platform-wide numbers: pages average 11.1 views each, and 48.3% of views are on a phone.

**Cut first:** duplicate photographs. Three shots of one evening is one photo.

## What length research actually shows about being believed

Here is the inconvenient finding, and it cuts against everything above: length buys credibility.

In an EEG study of 105 participants judging translations of unfamiliar Kanji signs, long notes were accepted as true in 4,079 of 7,605 trials — 53.6% — against 3,455 of 8,432 for short notes, or 41.0%. A binomial test returned p < 0.000001, and the authors name it outright as [a cognitive bias for long notes](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8485696/) (Frontiers in Human Neuroscience, 17 September 2021).

So more words do make a claim more believable. The catch is that a proposal is not a claim. Nobody is auditing whether you mean it; they are deciding whether to spend a life with you, and another sentence is not evidence toward that decision.

The other direction is measured too. In Gray and Leary's 1935 study, in which about 800 adults were tested on 48 passages, average sentence length in words correlated −.52 with reading ease — the longer the sentence, the harder the passage — as recorded in [DuBay's 2004 survey of readability research](https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED490073.pdf). Length helps you be believed and hurts you being understood, and in a proposal only the second is in play.

## Why length has to survive being put down

Sampled on the apology dashboard template, the median gap between a page's first save and its last edit is 2.2 hours, n=1,375.

That is a writer's behaviour, not a reader's, and we have no equivalent measurement of reading. It is still useful: whoever builds one of these does not do it in a single pass, and there is no reason to assume the reader will either.

The consequence is a length rule, not a design rule. Anything long enough to be put down halfway has to still make sense when it is picked up, and below about three screens that problem does not arise. That is the argument for the shorter end of every range here.

## How the four forms compare

One row per form, with what we can measure from our side and what we cannot.

| Form | Length limit | Traceable to | Platform-wide signal |
|---|---|---|---|
| Spoken ask | 45–90 words, then the question | 196 WPM conversational rate, Interspeech 2006 | None — we measure pages, not speech |
| Written message | ~60 words, three sentences | 20-word modern sentence average, DuBay 2004, plus editorial judgement | 48.3% of views on a phone, across 21 page types |
| Letter | one 15–20 minute sitting | expressive writing protocol, Baikie & Wilhelm 2005 | 2.2 h median first-save to last-edit, sampled on /apology-dashboard, n=1,375 |
| Built page | 3–5 screens | editorial judgement | 11.1 average views per created page |

The takeaway: only the spoken row rests on a hard external number, and only the two screen-based rows carry our own. Nothing in the table is a proposal-specific measurement, because we have none.

## When a longer proposal is right, and when one sentence beats all four

A scrapbook is the long form and it suits a narrow reader: someone with years of material and a partner who will sit and scroll. Our [marry-me proposal scrapbook page](/proposal) runs your story to a YES button that grows every time they dodge it. Length is the point of that format — use it when the story is long, not when it is not.

A two-month relationship on a scrapbook reads as padding, which is the thing this whole page is about removing.

Most people searching this in India are not asking about marriage at all. In Indian usage "propose" usually means asking someone to be your girlfriend or boyfriend, and that ask wants a shorter frame: the ["I love you" page](/love-gf) is sized for it, and it is our most-viewed template at 16,998 views, 29.9% of all page views platform-wide.

Two sibling posts cover what this one leaves out. [How to write a propose message for her](/blog/propose-message-for-her) is the drafting process — incubation, revision, what to cut.

[Building an online proposal for a girlfriend](/blog/online-proposal-for-girlfriend) is the conditions a page is read in, including what belongs on the first screen. This page is only about how much.

The honest case against all of it: if you are in the same room and you already know the answer, one spoken sentence beats every format here, ours included. A page is for distance, for a story worth scrolling, or for a moment someone will reopen. It is not for a question you can ask in eight words.

## Sources

- Yuan, Liberman and Cieri, ["Towards an Integrated Understanding of Speaking Rate in Conversation"](https://www.isca-archive.org/interspeech_2006/yuan06_interspeech.html), Interspeech 2006.
- ["What to Believe? Impact of Knowledge and Message Length on Neural Activity in Message Credibility Evaluation"](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8485696/), Frontiers in Human Neuroscience, 17 September 2021.
- Baikie and Wilhelm, ["Emotional and physical health benefits of expressive writing"](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/advances-in-psychiatric-treatment/article/emotional-and-physical-health-benefits-of-expressive-writing/ED2976A61F5DE56B46F07A1CE9EA9F9F), Advances in Psychiatric Treatment, 2005.
- DuBay, ["The Principles of Readability"](https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED490073.pdf), 2004.

Europe PMC returned an HTML error page on every call from this machine, so the Europe PMC half of findpapers.mjs produced nothing; link.springer.com was behind a Cloudflare client challenge and its persuasion-and-length paper was rejected rather than cited unread.

Source 3 (Baikie and Wilhelm 2005) was read as the open Cambridge Core HTML - abstract plus the body passages describing the expressive-writing paradigm. The PDF was not downloaded. The article is open, not paywalled.
